config.title: List Rendering with map()

intro.title: List Rendering with map()
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a React component that displays a dynamic list of items, such as a todo list or product catalog. You'll learn how to use JavaScript's map() method to transform an array of data into an array of JSX elements, which is the foundation of list rendering in React. The lesson covers the essential React concept of rendering lists dynamically, using the map() function to iterate through data and the key prop to help React efficiently update the DOM. You'll work with JavaScript arrays, JSX syntax, and React's rendering system to create components that can display any number of items from your data. By the end, you'll understand how to take raw data and transform it into a user interface that automatically updates when your data changes.
intro.usecase: List rendering with map() is fundamental to modern web applications, powering dynamic content like product catalogs on e-commerce sites, user feeds on social media platforms, and data tables in admin dashboards. You'll use this pattern to display search results, render navigation menus, show comment threads, or create todo lists where the number of items changes based on user interaction or API responses. Every time you see a repeating UI element that displays different data - like Netflix movie rows, GitHub repository lists, or Slack message threads - it's likely implemented using map() to transform an array of data into JSX elements. This makes it one of the most essential React patterns for building scalable, data-driven interfaces.

objectives: Apply the map() method to transform an array of data into JSX elements
Implement key props correctly when rendering lists of components
Construct dynamic list components that render varying amounts of data
Configure conditional rendering within mapped list items
Manipulate array data structures to generate interactive UI elements
Integrate event handlers into dynamically rendered list components
Control the display of nested data properties within mapped elements

steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React from the 'react' package.

import React from 'react'

steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! React is now imported and ready to use.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're importing React from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React from 'react' to use React components and JSX.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now
steps.hint: Define a function named App that returns null - you can use either function declaration or arrow function syntax
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is created that returns null
successCriteria: App component is defined as a function that returns null
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your component is named 'App' and returns null for now.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a function named 'App' that returns null. You can use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.

steps.title: Initialize the fruits array data
steps.instruction: Create an array variable named 'fruits' containing at least three fruit names as strings
steps.hint: Declare a variable using const and assign it an array with string values like ['apple', 'banana', 'orange']
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating an array of colors
const colors = ['red', 'blue', 'green'];
steps.expectedOutcome: A fruits array is created with multiple fruit name strings that will be used for list rendering
successCriteria: A variable named 'fruits' is declared as an array containing at least three string values representing fruit names
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your array is named 'fruits' and contains at least three fruit names as strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create an array variable named 'fruits' with string values representing different fruit names.

steps.title: Return basic JSX structure
steps.instruction: Return a div container with an h1 heading that displays 'My Favorite Fruits'
steps.hint: Use return statement to return JSX. Wrap your elements in a div and add an h1 element inside.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a div containing an h1 heading with the text 'My Favorite Fruits'
successCriteria: Component returns JSX with a div wrapper and h1 heading displaying 'My Favorite Fruits'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're returning JSX with both a div wrapper and an h1 heading inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the return statement to return JSX from your component. Include a div wrapper with an h1 heading inside.

steps.title: Add the map() method to render list items
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the map() method on the fruits array to create <li> elements for each fruit
steps.hint: Use fruits.map() and return an <li> element containing each fruit name. Remember to include a key prop for each list item.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fruits array is mapped to create <li> elements inside the <ul>, with each fruit displayed as a list item
successCriteria: The map() method is used on the fruits array to generate <li> elements with proper key props
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're using the map() method on the fruits array and returning <li> elements. Don't forget to add a key prop to each list item.
steps.feedbackWrong:
use the map() method on your fruits array. The syntax is fruits.map(fruit =>

      tags.

steps.title: Add key prop to each list item
steps.instruction: Add a key prop to each li element using the array index as the unique identifier
steps.hint: In the map function, you can access the index as the second parameter: map((item, index) => ...). Then add key={index} to your li element.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: using index as key in map students.map((student, index) =>

{student}

)
steps.expectedOutcome: Each list item will have a unique key prop using the array index, preventing React warnings about missing keys
successCriteria: Each li element has a key prop with the index value from the map function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure each li element has a key prop set to the index parameter from the map function.
steps.feedbackWrong: add the key prop to your li elements. Use the index parameter from the map function as the key value.

steps.title: Fix the key prop by adding it to the li element
steps.instruction: Add the key prop to each li element using the index parameter from the map function
steps.hint: The key prop should be added as key={index} to help React track each list item efficiently
steps.expectedOutcome: Each list item will have a key prop set to its index, which helps React efficiently update the list when it changes
successCriteria: The li element includes key={index} prop
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the key prop is added to the li element and uses the index parameter from the map function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The key prop is missing. Add key={index} to the li element to help React track each list item.

steps.title: Create an array of objects with more data
steps.instruction: Replace the fruits array with an array of fruit objects, where each object has 'name' and 'color' properties
steps.hint: Create an array where each element is an object with two properties: name (string) and color (string). For example: [{name: 'apple', color: 'red'}, ...]
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: array of person objects
const people = [{name: 'John', age: 25}, {name: 'Jane', age: 30}];
steps.expectedOutcome: The fruits variable now contains an array of objects, each with name and color properties
successCriteria: The fruits array contains objects with 'name' and 'color' properties instead of simple strings
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure each fruit object has both 'name' and 'color' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fruits array should contain objects, not strings. Each object needs 'name' and 'color' properties.

steps.title: Update the map() to display object properties
steps.instruction: Modify the map() callback function to display both the name and color properties from each fruit object instead of just the fruit string
steps.hint: Access object properties using dot notation (e.g., fruit.name and fruit.color) and display them together in the list item
steps.expectedOutcome: The list items will display both the name and color of each fruit (e.g., 'apple - red') instead of '[object Object]'
successCriteria: The map() callback accesses and displays both fruit.name and fruit.color properties within each list item
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track accessing object properties. Make sure to display both the name and color properties from each fruit object.
steps.feedbackWrong: use dot notation to access object properties. Try displaying fruit.name and fruit.color within the list item JSX.

steps.title: Export the App component
steps.instruction: Add a default export statement for the App component at the end of the file
steps.hint: Use 'export default' followed by the component name to make it available for import in other files
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: exporting a function
export default MyComponent;
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will be exported as the default export, making it available for import in other files
successCriteria: The App component is exported using 'export default App'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track with the export statement. Make sure you're using 'export default' followed by the component name 'App'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The export statement isn't quite right. You need to use 'export default App' to make the component available for import in other files.
